Science.title: BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03803-8 European and Japanese probes will trace different paths around the planet to study its surface and its surroundings.

Science.title: Global analysis reveals how lakes amplify glacier ice loss
Science.summary: Glacial lakes can accelerate the retreat of glaciers. If glaciers border a lake, the water can melt the ice from underneath; furthermore, chunks of ice can break off and fall into the lake. The extent to which these processes influence the situation, compared with other factors, had not been sufficiently clarified at a global level until now.

Science.title: Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions
Science.summary: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north.

Science.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
Science.summary: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy. NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed […]

Science.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
Science.summary: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. Rather, it will go on display as a museum piece, according to company founder and CEO Elon Musk.

Science.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
Science.summary: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

Science.title: Parasite protein expands understanding of how mitochondria build their ribosomes
Science.summary: Mitochondria are essential components of the cells of most organisms, including humans. They are often referred to as the cell's powerhouses because they produce the energy needed for cellular functions. However, mitochondria originally evolved from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by other cells in the distant past.

Science.title: Repeated bending strengthens sugar-based hydrogel instead of wearing it down
Science.summary: Most materials get weaker with use. But a team led by Chenfeng Ke, a professor of chemistry in Arts & Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis, has created a polymer that defies the usual laws of wear and tear.

Science.title: An ancient failed rift is reawakening inside one of Africa's oldest landmasses
Science.summary: In April 2017, a magnitude 6.5 earthquake shook southern Africa from an unlikely place: the middle of the Kalahari Craton in eastern Botswana. Cratons are the ancient cores of continents, and this one is built from blocks of crust up to 3.7 billion years old. Geologists have long considered such regions too cold, too thick and too rigid to tear apart.

Science.title: Tested on mushrooms, an AI model shows potential for detecting crop stress with far fewer computations
Science.summary: A new artificial intelligence (AI) model can detect stress in agricultural crops using a nondestructive imaging technique, allowing changes in crop health to be monitored over time. Developed by a team of researchers at Penn State, the new model shows promise for accurately detecting crop stress caused by drought, disease, nutrient deficiency and other causes while using less computing power than some existing AI methods.

Science.title: Scientists discover twist-tunable interlayer excitons in atomically thin anisotropic semiconductors
Science.summary: When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE).

Science.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
Science.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

Science.title: Record-setting X-ray laser reliably generates flashes with wavelengths shorter than distances between atoms
Science.summary: Researchers from DESY and European XFEL have demonstrated reliable production and transport of X-ray laser flashes with a wavelength of about 0.04 nanometers (or a photon energy of 30,000 electronvolts) at European XFEL, raising their own world record. This means that the X-ray's wavelength is much shorter than typical distances between neighboring atoms in solids, which enables the study of materials with higher spatial resolution than before.

Science.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California (video)
Science.summary: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

Science.title: Waterfall of fog spills over Mallorca cliffs in stunning winning image for Weather Photographer of the Year 2026
Science.summary: A spectacular sea of fog, a perfectly formed rainbow and dramatic lightning strikes feature among this year's winning photographs for Weather Photographer of the Year 2026.

Science.title: Caribbean corals are in crisis. Fossil reefs can help point to where corals may persist
Science.summary: The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years. Those fossils could help show where corals might survive a warming future. In two new papers, researchers at The University of Texas at Austin identify which coral species dominated ancient reefs in northeastern Jamaica and suggest how that record could guide reef rehabilitation.

Science.title: X-ray technique advances temperature measurements under extreme pressure
Science.summary: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), providing new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high-energy-density physics.

Science.title: People wade through floodwater because they underestimate danger—how to avoid risk
Science.summary: A footpath home disappears beneath brown water. The other side is only a few meters away and someone has already crossed. Turning back means a long detour and you will be late. Would you wade through? This is the kind of everyday decision that flood safety advice must address.

Science.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
Science.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

Science.title: 'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest big-screen adventure
Science.summary: Assimilate this! How cyber-zombies and the "birth of 'Star Trek'" gave Jean-Luc Picard one of his finest hours.

Science.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
Science.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

Science.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
Science.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

Science.title: A million tiny crystals reveal how semiconductors form distinct cores and shells
Science.summary: Perovskites and related materials called perovskitoids are promising semiconductor materials for solar cells, LEDs and light detectors. Their ingredients and internal crystal structures determine how they absorb and emit light. A chip just 2 centimeters across can hold roughly a million tiny crystals—becoming a miniature material library that can show how some mixtures separate into distinct cores and shells, changing the light they absorb.

Science.title: The avian champions of long-distance migration keep surprising scientists
Science.summary: "The whole story began with an extinct bird from Hispaniola," said Min Zhao, a former postdoctoral associate at the Florida Museum of Natural History (now a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University).

Science.title: Dropping degree requirements linked to higher pay for workers without degrees
Science.summary: The requirements set by human resources (HR) greatly influence the professional opportunities available to different segments of the population. For instance, if a job requires applicants to have earned a bachelor's or master's degree in a relevant subject, people without them may be excluded from the selection process, even if they have gained relevant skills through experience or professional training.

Science.title: The call of the seamount: Two new armored tardigrades described in the Atlantic
Science.summary: An international team led by researchers from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven has described two new species of marine tardigrades. The tiny marine organisms were discovered in the sediment of the Senghor Seamount off the coast of Cape Verde. According to the researchers, the discovery underscores the role of undersea mountains as oases of biodiversity. The study, which includes comprehensive taxonomic descriptions of the new species, has been published in the journal "ZooKeys."

Science.title: Curiosity Spots Drifting Twilight Clouds
Science.summary: Description NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured these drifting clouds on Oct. 31, 2026, the 5,061st Martian day, or sol, of the mission. The rover uses its navigation cameras to capture post-sunset clouds, called twilight clouds, which appear for only a short time each fall over Gale Crater, which it has been exploring for more than […]

Science.title: Scientists put 78,000 letters of human DNA into a mouse — and unraveled how a rare disease worked
Science.summary: By inserting human genes into lab mice, scientists were able to study the underlying mechanics of a disease that's been notoriously difficult to research.

Science.title: Babies in ancient Greek colony started solid food at 3 months but nursed for nearly 4 years, chemical signatures suggest
Science.summary: Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks. Despite their diverse cultural backgrounds, they all shared one thing: they began weaning their babies early and continued for a long time.

Science.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
Science.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

Science.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
Science.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

Science.title: A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years
Science.summary: Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state.

Science.title: Quantum software matches classical benchmark for a molecular interaction
Science.summary: Predicting how molecules interact is central to drug discovery: it offers important information about how a new drug might work in the human body, the side effects it can cause and more. Computationally modeling these interactions can reduce the need for lengthy and expensive lab work, but some interactions still remain beyond the reach of classical computers.

Science.title: GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars
Science.summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally out, but if you're a sci-fi aficionado looking for similar experiences set in outer space, there are several alternatives.

Science.title: Broadening the role of RNA: A messenger, a mediator and now a condensate coordinator
Science.summary: New research about condensates—cellular compartments that act as hubs for facilitating biological reactions—continues to reveal novel insights into how cells function. Among those continuing to push the field forward are members of the Marine Biological Laboratory's condensate consortium, including Amy Gladfelter, a professor at Duke University and current co-director of the MBL physiology course, and former MBL physiology course student and past MBL Whitman fellow Dragomir Milovanovic, a professor at the Charité Berlin University Institute of Biochemistry.

Science.title: Mapping the microbes' arms race with viruses at planetary scale
Science.summary: Microbiomes are complex ecosystems, in which bacteria and archaea are constantly interacting with, and infected by, viruses. These viruses can significantly impact microbiome processes, not only by killing their host but also sometimes by temporarily providing additional capabilities to their host. As many viruses have not been grown in a lab, connecting them to their natural hosts has been difficult. A new bioinformatics toolkit and database are now available to help researchers make those associations at an unprecedented scale.

Science.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
Science.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

Science.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
Science.summary: Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing the lunar environment may suffer irreversible damage if things move too fast.

Science.title: Digital imaging workshop aims to reveal secrets in medieval manuscripts
Science.summary: Researchers recently used multispectral imaging technology to try to uncover hidden information from medieval manuscripts at the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The library hosted a digital imaging workshop in early October that served as a pilot study for how the technology can help analyze fragile, centuries-old documents.

Science.title: New hemp plant produces no detectable THC, potentially reducing risk of crop destruction
Science.summary: Scientists at Texas A M AgriLife Research, a member of The Texas A M University System, have developed a hemp plant that produces no detectable cannabinoids, including THC.

Science.title: 'A future where EVs charge simply by parking': New positioning system could make wireless EV charging much more efficient
Science.summary: A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

Science.title: Can Instagram reduce prejudice? Study reveals the potential and limits of social media contact
Science.summary: A research team at the University of Potsdam has conducted a field experiment to investigate whether contact through social media can reduce prejudice. The findings suggest that following an unfamiliar Instagram profile for just three days can lead to more favorable attitudes—not only toward the group represented by the profile. The study was published in the Journal of the Association for Information Systems.

Science.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
Science.summary: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.

Science.title: Brains of people with PTSD have unique epigenetic marks, study finds
Science.summary: The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

Science.title: From screens in class to smart glasses, Norway rethinks new technologies
Science.summary: Three years ago, a schoolteacher in Norway was reprimanded for putting his pupils' iPads aside to return to pen and paper. Now, the whole country is rethinking its approach to new technologies.

Science.title: Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders
Science.summary: Resilient strawberry varieties will be more easily identifiable thanks to a tool developed by University of Queensland engineering students. The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin, a key breeding consideration for the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries.

Science.title: Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches
Science.summary: Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey orbiter is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work by the end of November.

Science.title: Gamified mobile payment features may drive adoption among Gen-Z users
Science.summary: Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical ways, according to research published in the International Journal of Business Information Systems.

Science.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
Science.summary: Aldebaran looks for all the world like the brightest member of the Hyades star cluster. It isn't — and discovering why changes the way you look at constellations.

Science.title: Why do wolves howl?
Science.summary: Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

Science.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
Science.summary: We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

Science.title: Meet the science adviser behind Netflix's hit series 'Below'
Science.summary: Live Science spoke with marine biologist Annie Mercier about her role as a science adviser for Netflix's show "Below."
